common_name: Ailsa Craig Tomato (Classic Scottish Heirloom Slicer)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Ailsa Craig is a compact-vined indeterminate variety long favored in Scottish and English glasshouses and outdoor gardens alike, so it appreciates staking and consistent moisture through fruit set.

directions: Sow seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil once nights stay reliably above 50 degrees F, staking or caging the vines as they grow. Ailsa Craig was bred in Girvan, Scotland in the early 1900s and quickly became one of the most widely grown tomatoes in British gardens and allotments, prized for producing heavy clusters of medium, smooth, bright red fruit with a well-balanced, classic tomato flavor. It remains a benchmark variety in the UK for home growers wanting a dependable, flavorful, mid-sized slicer.

common_name: Alicante Tomato (British Garden and Greenhouse Slicer)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Alicante sets fruit reliably in cooler summers and short seasons, making it a mainstay of British allotments and greenhouses.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once temperatures are reliably warm, providing a stake or cage for the indeterminate vines. Alicante is a long-established open-pollinated British variety known for consistent early cropping and smooth, medium-sized, deep red fruit with a well-rounded, sweet-tart flavor that holds up in cooler, shorter growing seasons. It has been a staple recommendation of UK seed catalogs and gardening programs for decades as a reliable outdoor and unheated-greenhouse tomato.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; German Pink is a vigorous potato-leaved indeterminate that benefits from sturdy staking to support its large fruit.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply into warm soil, staking or caging the sprawling vines. German Pink descends from seed brought from Bavaria to Iowa in 1883 by the family of Seed Savers Exchange co-founder Diane Ott Whealy, and it produces huge, meaty, nearly seedless pink-skinned fruit with a mild, sweet flavor well suited to slicing and canning alike. It remains one of the founding heirloom varieties associated with the Seed Savers Exchange movement.

common_name: Eva Purple Ball Tomato (German Black Forest Heirloom)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Eva Purple Ball is noted for holding up well in hot, humid conditions and shows useful foliar disease tolerance in the garden.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil, staking the indeterminate vines as they grow. Eva Purple Ball traces to Germany's Black Forest region in the late 1800s and was carried to New Jersey by the Bratka family, producing smooth, round, rosy-pink fruit of five to seven ounces with a sweet, well-balanced flavor. Gardeners in hot, humid regions especially value it for staying productive and relatively blemish-free when many other heirlooms struggle with disease pressure.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Nebraska Wedding grows on relatively compact plants that still benefit from a stake or cage as fruit loads increase.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once soil has warmed, providing support for the fruit-laden branches. This variety was carried by pioneer families from Minnesota to the Nebraska plains in the late 1800s, and tradition held that a pinch of its seed was given to Nebraska brides as a wedding gift so they could grow it in their own gardens. The plants yield deep orange, globe-shaped fruit with a rich, sweet flavor and few seeds, and the variety was later documented and preserved through the Seed Savers Exchange network.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Cuostralee is a regular-leaf indeterminate that needs sturdy staking to hold up its one- to two-pound fruit.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply into warm, fertile soil, staking firmly to support the heavy fruit. Cuostralee is an old French family heirloom obtained from a grower in Hellimer, France in 1992 by American tomato collectors Craig LeHoullier and Carolyn Male, who helped introduce it to North American gardeners. Its deeply ribbed, pink-red fruit can top a pound or more per tomato and is known for dense, meaty flesh and a rich, old-fashioned sweet flavor.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; harvest fruit while still pale orange-yellow just before frost for the longest storage life, rather than waiting for vine-ripening.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil, caging or staking the semi-sprawling vines. Long Keeper is grown specifically for its ability to ripen slowly off the vine when picked mature-green to pale blush before the first fall frost, gradually coloring to an orange-red over weeks or months in cool, dark storage so gardeners can enjoy fresh tomatoes well into winter. The flavor is milder than a summer-ripened tomato but remains a valued novelty among gardeners who want to extend the tomato season past the growing year.

planting.note: Start indoors 6 weeks before transplanting; Oregon Spring can be set out slightly earlier than most tomatoes since it sets fruit at cooler temperatures than typical varieties.

directions: Start seed indoors about 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into the garden with minimal staking needed, since the compact determinate plants stay under three feet. Oregon Spring was bred by Dr. James Baggett at Oregon State University from a cross involving the cold-adapted Russian variety Severianin, and it was released in 1984 specifically for short, cool growing seasons in the Pacific Northwest and similar climates. The nearly seedless, medium-sized fruit sets even when nights stay chilly, giving gardeners in short-season regions a dependable early, low-acid harvest.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Wisconsin 55 is an indeterminate variety that benefits from staking to keep the disease-resistant foliage well aired.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil, staking or caging the vines for support. Wisconsin 55 was developed by plant pathologist J.C. Walker at the University of Wisconsin in the 1940s to resist early blight and leaf spot, and it went on to become one of the most popular home garden tomatoes in the upper Midwest through the mid-20th century. The round, deep red, six- to eight-ounce fruit is notably resistant to cracking and holds firm texture for slicing, canning, and cooking.

common_name: Micro Tom Tomato (Ultra-Dwarf Research and Container Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting; Micro Tom's extremely small size (under a foot tall) suits it to 4-6 inch pots, windowsills, and classroom or laboratory growing without any staking.

directions: Sow seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into a small pot once true leaves appear, since the plants never need staking and stay compact from seed to fruit. Micro-Tom was bred at the University of Florida from a cross of 'Florida Basket' and 'Ohio 4013-3' and carries a mutation that stunts its growth to just a few inches tall with a life cycle of only a few months, making it one of the most widely used model organisms in tomato genetics research worldwide. Home gardeners grow it mainly as a novelty for windowsills and tiny containers, where it still produces a modest crop of small, edible red fruit.
